jakarta: Jakarta lies on the north-western coast of Java at the mouth of the Ciliwung river, facing Jakarta Bay. It covers about 664 square kilometres of land. Apart from some hills in the south, the city spreads across low, flat terrain, much of it an alluvial plain with elevations from below sea level to about 50 metres. Thirteen rivers run through it toward the bay. The plain was historically swampy, and seasonal flooding remains common.

The Buni culture, a prehistoric pottery culture of the northern and western coast of Java, is dated to roughly 400 BCE to 100 CE. The mid-5th-century Tugu inscription, found near Tanjung Priok, records the excavation of two waterways and attributes one of them to King Purnawarman. By the 10th century the Sunda Kingdom ruled the area, and by the early 16th century Kalapa was one of its leading ports. The Portuguese writer Tomé Pires called it Sunda's most important trading port, drawing ships from Sumatra, Malacca and Java. A treaty of 21 August 1522 allowed the Portuguese to build a fortress at Kalapa.

In 1527 Islamic forces captured Kalapa, and sources differ over whether Fatahillah or Sunan Gunung Jati led them. The settlement became a dependency of the Banten Sultanate under the name Jayakarta. The Dutch East India Company seized and destroyed Jayakarta in 1619 and rebuilt it as Batavia, its main administrative centre in Asia and an important trading port. In the early 19th century the Dutch colonial administration moved south to Weltevreden.

Indonesian independence was proclaimed in Jakarta in 1945, and after the Indonesian National Revolution it became the capital of the unitary republic in 1950. It became a first-level region in 1957 and a Special Capital Region in 1961. In 2022 the Indonesian government began the legal process of moving the capital to Nusantara in East Kalimantan.

Jakarta is the capital and largest city of Indonesia, with the status of a province, and had about 11 million registered residents in 2025. No ethnic group forms a majority; Javanese, Betawi, Sundanese and Chinese Indonesians are the largest. The Betawi people formed in colonial Batavia from people of varied origins. Indonesian is the official language, and the city hosts the headquarters of ASEAN. Its Old Town keeps the historic core.
jamaica: Jamaica covers 10,991 square kilometres and is the third-largest island in the Greater Antilles and the Caribbean, after Cuba and Hispaniola. It lies about 145 km south of Cuba and 191 km west of Hispaniola. Mountains dominate the interior, among them the Blue Mountains in the east, where Blue Mountain Peak rises to 2,256 metres, and a narrow coastal plain surrounds them. The island lies within the main development region for Atlantic tropical cyclones and sometimes suffers heavy storm damage. When the Spanish arrived in 1494 the country was deeply forested, and European settlers later cleared much of it for timber and cultivation.

There is no archaeological evidence of human presence until about 500 CE. A group known as the Redware people, after their pottery, arrived around 600 CE, followed by the Taíno around 800 CE, who most likely came from South America. The Taíno lived by farming and fishing, and at their height are thought to have numbered some 60,000 people in around 200 villages headed by caciques. Christopher Columbus claimed the island for Spain after landing in 1494 on his second voyage. The first Spanish settlement, Sevilla, was founded in 1509 by Juan de Esquivel and abandoned around 1524; the capital moved to Spanish Town, then St. Jago de la Vega, around 1534.

The Taíno died in large numbers from introduced diseases and from enslavement by the Spanish, who then imported enslaved Africans. Many escaped and formed autonomous communities in the remote interior, mixing with the remaining Taíno; these became the Jamaican Maroons, who kept their freedom for generations under leaders such as Juan de Serras. By the early 17th century an estimated 2,500 to 3,000 people lived on the island.

England conquered Jamaica from Spain in 1655. Under British rule it became a leading sugar exporter, with a plantation economy that depended on importing enslaved Africans. The British emancipated all slaves in 1838, and many freedmen chose subsistence farms over plantation work. From the 1840s the British brought Chinese and Indian indentured labourers. Independence from the United Kingdom came on 6 August 1962.

Jamaica is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a Commonwealth realm, with a bicameral Parliament, and its constitution dates from 1962. The capital and largest city is Kingston. Most Jamaicans are of African or partly African descent, with minorities of European, Indian, Chinese and Lebanese origin. The Maroon communities of Accompong and elsewhere continue to keep their own traditions. The island is the birthplace of the Rastafari religion and of reggae, ska, dub and dancehall music, and its national motto is Out of Many One People.
james-joyce: James Joyce was born on 2 February 1882 in Rathgar, Dublin, the eldest of ten surviving siblings. His father, John Stanislaus Joyce, was appointed rate collector by Dublin Corporation in 1887, but his unpredictable finances made family life chaotic. Joyce attended Clongowes Wood College and Belvedere College, and in 1898 enrolled at University College, Dublin, to study English, French and Italian, graduating in 1902. There he met the scholasticism of Thomas Aquinas, which influenced his thought for the rest of his life. He lapsed from the Catholic Church early, though his work is deeply influenced by Catholicism.

In October 1904 Joyce and Nora Barnacle went into self-imposed exile. He taught English in Pola and then Trieste, then part of Austria-Hungary, worked for eight months as a correspondence clerk in a Roman bank, and lived in Trieste until 1915, publishing Chamber Music and Dubliners there. He spent most of the First World War in Zurich, supported by a stipend that Pound and Yeats helped arrange and by regular sums from the editor Harriet Shaw Weaver, who supported him for the rest of his life.

In 1920 he moved to Paris, his main home for twenty years. Sylvia Beach, who ran the bookshop Shakespeare and Company, became one of his publishers. Ulysses was first published in Paris in 1922; its publication in the United Kingdom and the United States was prohibited as obscene, and copies were smuggled in and pirated until the mid-1930s, when publication became legal. He began Finnegans Wake in 1923, and suffered increasingly severe eye problems.

When Germany occupied France in 1940, Joyce moved back to Zurich. He underwent surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer on 11 January 1941 and died on 13 January, aged 58. Though he spent most of his adult life abroad, his fiction centres on Dublin. Ulysses is a model for fiction writers, and Finnegans Wake has become one of the key texts for French post-structuralism. His work and life are marked each year on 16 June, known as Bloomsday, in Dublin and in a growing number of other cities.
jane-austen: Jane Austen was born on 16 December 1775 in Steventon, Hampshire. Her father, George Austen, was the rector of the Anglican parishes of Steventon and Deane. He came from an old and wealthy family of wool merchants, but his own branch fell into poverty as each generation's eldest sons received the inheritances, and he was orphaned as a child. At sixteen he entered St John's College, Oxford, where he most likely met Cassandra Leigh, who came from the prominent Leigh family.

In 1809 her brother Edward offered his mother and sisters the use of a large cottage in Chawton, and Jane, Cassandra and their mother moved there on 7 July 1809. Life was quieter there than at any time since the family's move to Bath in 1800.

Austen wrote major novels before the age of 22 but was not published until she was 35. Like many women authors of her time she published anonymously. The ideal roles for a woman were then wife and mother, and a woman who wished to be a full-time writer was felt to be degrading her femininity. Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814) and Emma (1815) were moderate successes but did not bring her public fame in her lifetime.

Sir Walter Scott wrote an anonymous review of Emma in 1815, praising her realism. She died on 18 July 1817. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published after her death, and her brother Henry Austen's Biographical Note, dated December 1817, first identified her as the author of the novels. She left unfinished the novel Sanditon.

Austen's six novels implicitly interpret and criticise the English landed gentry at the end of the 18th century. Her plots often explore the dependence of women on marriage for social standing and economic security. Her works critique the sentimental novels of the second half of the 18th century and are part of the transition to 19th-century literary realism. Critics have praised her social commentary, wit and irony.

In 1832 Richard Bentley bought the remaining copyrights to her novels and in October 1833 released the first collected edition, in his Standard Novels series. Her novels have been continuously in print since. Her nephew published A Memoir of Jane Austen in 1869.
japan: Japan is an island country in East Asia, made up of 14,125 islands that stretch over 3,000 kilometres along the Pacific coast of Asia. The five main islands, from north to south, are Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and Okinawa. About 75% of the terrain is mountainous and heavily forested, so the population is concentrated on the coastal plains. Japan lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire and is prone to earthquakes, tsunami and volcanic eruptions; the 1923 Tokyo earthquake killed over 140,000 people, and the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake triggered a large tsunami.

The first known habitation dates to the Upper Paleolithic. The Jōmon period began around 14,500 BCE, and the Yayoi people later entered the archipelago from the Korean Peninsula, bringing wet-rice farming and metallurgy. According to legend, Emperor Jimmu founded a kingdom in central Japan in 660 BCE. Japan first appears in written history in the Chinese Book of Han, completed in 111 CE. Buddhism was introduced from Baekje in 552, and in 645 the Taika Reforms aimed at greater centralisation of power in the imperial court, on the model of China.

From the 12th century actual power was held by military aristocrats known as shōgun and feudal lords called daimyō. After the Kamakura and Ashikaga shogunates and a century of warring states, the Tokugawa shogunate unified the country in 1600 and implemented an isolationist foreign policy. An American fleet forced Japan to open trade in 1853, which led to the end of the shogunate and the restoration of imperial power in 1868. Japan annexed Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910, invaded China in 1937 and entered World War II as an Axis power in 1941. It surrendered in 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and was under Allied occupation until 1952.

Japan has a population of nearly 123 million, and Tokyo is the capital and largest city. It is a constitutional monarchy in which the emperor's role is ceremonial, and its legislature is the bicameral National Diet. The Constitution of Japan was adopted in 1947. Minority groups include the indigenous Ainu and Ryukyuan people.
jaswant-singh-of-marwar: Jaswant Singh was born on 26 December 1626 at Burhanpur, the youngest son of Maharaja Gaj Singh of Marwar. He succeeded on 6 May 1638 by special decree of Emperor Shah Jahan and was installed at Mehrangarh in Jodhpur on 25 May 1638. His father's favourite concubine, Anara Begum, who regarded him as her own son and was at odds with the heir apparent Amar Singh Rathore, had a part in his accession; Amar Singh was later given Nagore in compensation. He held in jagir the parganas of Jodhpur, Siwana, Merta, Sojat, Phalodi and Pokharan, and Shah Jahan granted him the personal title of Maharaja on 6 January 1654.

Shah Jahan sent him to stop the advance of the rebel princes Aurangzeb and Murad. The armies met at Dharmatpur, fifteen miles from Ujjain, on 15 April 1658. His advisers proposed a night raid on Aurangzeb's artillery and gunpowder, since the Rajput army was almost wholly light cavalry; he is quoted as answering that it was inconsistent with the manliness of the Rajputs to employ stratagems or make a night attack. He was defeated and lost 6,000 men, among them Ratan Singh Rathore of Ratlam and Mokand Das Hada of Kota.

Posted to the Deccan, he made Pune his headquarters. In 1664 he besieged Kondana without success, and he left for Delhi after Jai Singh was sent to the Deccan. He returned in 1667 with Prince Muazzam, the new viceroy, and acted as an intermediary between Shivaji and Aurangzeb. In 1670 he was posted at Burhanpur.

His son Prithviraj Singh died at Delhi on 8 May 1667; the khyats, the chronicles of Marwar, say that Aurangzeb had given him a poisoned robe. Jaswant Singh died at Jamrud, near Peshawar, on a date usually converted as 28 December 1678, though another scholar makes it 28 November 1678. Two of his wives were pregnant at his death and both bore sons, which led to a war over the installation of Ajit Singh Rathore as ruler of Marwar. He was also a man of letters, the author of the Siddhant-Bodh, the Anand Vilas and the Bhasha-Bhushan.
jawaharlal-nehru: Jawaharlal Nehru was born on 14 November 1889 in Allahabad to Swarup Rani and Motilal Nehru, a wealthy, self-made barrister who served as president of the Indian National Congress in 1919 and 1928. Both parents were Kashmiri Pandits. Nehru grew up in the mansion Anand Bhavan and was educated at home by governesses and tutors. He became an ardent nationalist in his youth, stirred by the Second Boer War and the Russo-Japanese War.

He was educated at Harrow School and Trinity College, Cambridge, from which he graduated in 1910 with an honours degree in natural science, and trained in the law at the Inner Temple. After returning to India in August 1912 he enrolled at the Allahabad High Court, but had little interest in the law, and nationalist politics gradually replaced his practice.

Nehru met Mahatma Gandhi in 1916. During the non-cooperation movement of 1920 he directed political activity in the United Provinces, and on 6 December 1921 he was imprisoned for the first of eight periods of detention between 1921 and 1945, lasting over nine years in all. He pressed the Congress to break all ties with the British Empire, and as its president at the Lahore session on 29 December 1929 he introduced a successful resolution calling for complete independence.

The Congress swept the 1937 provincial elections under his leadership. After the Quit India Resolution of 8 August 1942, senior Congress leaders were imprisoned, and in their absence the Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah grew in power.

Nehru became interim prime minister in September 1946. On 15 August 1947 he gave the speech Tryst with Destiny and was sworn in as prime minister of the Dominion of India, and on 26 January 1950 he became first prime minister of the Republic. He held office for 16 years and 286 days, and the Congress won the elections of 1951, 1957 and 1962 under him.

In 1961 the Indian Army invaded Portuguese-controlled Goa, which he formally annexed. From 1959 his Forward Policy set up military outposts in disputed territory on the Sino-Indian border, and China attacked some of them, beginning the Sino-Indian War of 1962, which India lost. He died in office in 1964.

Bhikhu Parekh regards Nehru as the founder of the modern Indian state, for the national philosophy of modernisation he formulated, with goals including national unity, parliamentary democracy, industrialisation, socialism, the scientific temper and non-alignment. He advocated a mixed economy, with a government-controlled public sector coexisting with private industry, and directed investment into steel, iron, coal and power. In December 1953 he appointed the States Reorganisation Commission to prepare states on linguistic lines. In foreign affairs he led the establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement. His books include An Autobiography (1936) and The Discovery of India (1946).
jayasimha-siddharaja: Jayasimha was the son of the Chaulukya king Karna and his Kadamba queen Mayanalladevi. The 14th-century author Merutunga has him seated on the throne at the age of three, on 7 January 1094, which would place his birth in 1091, but the story is absent from earlier writers and does not seem accurate. His courtier Hemachandra relates that Karna's nephew Devaprasada burned himself on Karna's funeral pyre. The historian A. K. Majumdar thinks this hides an unpleasant truth: that Devaprasada tried to usurp the throne from the young king and was killed by Mayanalladevi and her minister Santu, after which she ruled as regent.

Literary sources and inscriptions agree that he defeated Khangara, also called Navaghana, king of Saurashtra; his Dahod inscription boasts that he imprisoned that king. He appointed Sajjana governor at Girnar, which an inscription of 1120 corroborates, but he could not take all of Khangara's lands.

Inscriptions disagree on whether the Paramara king he defeated was Naravarman or his successor Yashovarman. Majumdar holds that the war began under the first and ended under the second, and dates the capture of the Paramara capital Dhara to 1135-1136; the title Avantinatha, Lord of Avanti, first appears in an inscription of 1137. The Shakambhari Chahamana king Arnoraja, whom several sources say he subdued and to whom he gave his daughter Kanchana in marriage, helped him in this war, as did Asharaja of Naddula. Chaulukya chronicles claim that he then subdued the Chandela king Madanavarman, while a Chandela inscription claims the reverse, which suggests an inconclusive war.

He was a Shaivite who tolerated other faiths. Jains held important posts under him, and the Muslim historian Muhammad Aufi records that he inquired in person at Khambhat after a mosque was destroyed and eighty Muslims killed, and paid for its rebuilding. He renovated or rebuilt the Rudra Mahalaya Temple at Siddhapura, completed in 1142. The Sahastralinga lake was a renovation of one built by his ancestor Durlabha, ringed by 1008 small shrines each holding a linga. The grammar he commissioned from Hemachandra, the Siddha Hema Shabdanushasana, carries his name in its title.

Jayasimha had no son. According to Hemachandra he learned by divination that his grand-nephew Kumarapala would succeed him; later Jain chronicles say that he hated Kumarapala and persecuted him. It is not known how long he held Malwa. Bohra and Satpanth traditions claim that he was converted to Islam, but there is no evidence that he ever gave up Shaivism.
jean-jacques-rousseau: Rousseau was born on 28 June 1712 in the Republic of Geneva, a Protestant city-state and associate of the Swiss Confederacy that had been a Calvinist republic since 1536. His family belonged to the middle order of citizens with voting rights, and he generally signed his books Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Citizen of Geneva. In practice a small number of wealthy families ruled the city through its councils. When the reformer Pierre Fatio protested in 1707, he was shot by order of the Small Council, and Rousseau's grandfather, who had supported him, was penalised. His father, Isaac Rousseau, was a watchmaker, a former dance teacher and a lover of music.

Rousseau took formal music instruction at the house of Françoise-Louise de Warens, who housed him on and off for about 13 years. In 1742 he presented to the Académie des Sciences a system of musical notation using numbers, which they rejected while praising his effort. His first opera, Les Muses galantes, was written in 1743 and first performed in 1745. He wrote seven operas in all, the best known being the one-act The Village Soothsayer, composed in 1752. After 1752 he felt he could not go on working for the theatre.

A question set by the Academy of Dijon in 1750, whether the rebirth of the arts and sciences had purified morals, gave Rousseau what he called another universe. His essay in reply began his central argument that social and cultural progress had led to the moral degradation of humanity. In the Discourse on Inequality (1754) he held that private property is the source of social inequality. The Social Contract and Émile appeared in 1762, and Julie, or the New Heloise in 1761. Émile's endorsement of religious toleration led to its condemnation in both Calvinist Geneva and Catholic Paris.

In The Social Contract Rousseau described a legitimate political order resting on the general will, the collective will of a society as a whole, reached through the active involvement of every citizen in discussion and voting. The phrase was not original, since Diderot and Montesquieu had used it. During the French Revolution the Jacobin clubs invoked him in demanding equality, and Robespierre and Saint-Just took inspiration from him. His Confessions, completed in 1770, were published in 1782.
jean-paul-sartre: Jean-Paul Sartre was born on 21 June 1905 in Paris, the only child of Jean-Baptiste Sartre, a French Navy officer who died of an illness, most likely contracted in Indochina, when Sartre was two. He was raised at Meudon by his mother and his grandfather Charles Schweitzer, a teacher of German who introduced him to classical literature very early. As a teenager he was drawn to philosophy by Henri Bergson's Time and Free Will, and at the École Normale Supérieure he met Raymond Aron and Paul Nizan. In 1929 he met Simone de Beauvoir, and the two became lifelong companions in a relationship that was not monogamous.

During the Second World War Sartre was drafted, captured and later released, and then co-founded the resistance group Socialisme et Liberté. He wrote plays including The Flies and No Exit and became an influential voice in occupied France. After the war he co-founded the journal Les Temps modernes. He supported anti-colonial movements, condemned French policies in Algeria and opposed intervention in Vietnam. His friendship with Albert Camus ended after Camus's The Rebel (1951); Sartre believed violence was at times necessary for change. In 1964 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, which he tried to refuse, saying that a writer should not allow himself to be turned into an institution.

Sartre's central claim is that human beings are condemned to be free. Because there is no creator, humans have no essence before their existence: existence precedes essence. They cannot explain their actions by a fixed human nature and are fully responsible for them. Authenticity means facing the indeterminate character of existence in anguish; the inauthentic way flees that anguish by lying to oneself, which he called bad faith.

His principal philosophical work is Being and Nothingness (1943). Existentialism Is a Humanism (1946) began as a lecture, and his other works include the novel Nausea (1938), the play Dirty Hands (1948) and the autobiography The Words (1964). He died on 15 April 1980, and 50,000 mourners attended his funeral.
jesus: A Jewish person in the time of Jesus usually had only one name, sometimes followed by a patronymic or a home town, and so Jesus is commonly called Jesus of Nazareth in the New Testament. His name is the English transliteration, through Latin Iesus, of the Greek rendering of the Hebrew Yehoshua, shortened by that period to Yeshua; it means God saves. The word Christ is a title, not a given name, from the Greek Christos, meaning anointed, a calque of the Hebrew mashiakh, or messiah.

According to Christian tradition as represented in the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, Jesus was circumcised at eight days old and presented at the Temple in Jerusalem at 40 days. He was baptized by John the Baptist as a young adult. After 40 days and nights of fasting in the Judean wilderness he began his public ministry.

The four canonical gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, are the foremost sources for his life and message. By the usual scholarly view, Mark was written first, and Matthew and Luke used it as a source.

According to the New Testament accounts, Jesus was an itinerant teacher whom his followers believed to possess divine authority in interpreting Jewish law. He debated with other Jews, most commonly the Pharisees and Sadducees, engaged in healings, taught in parables, and gathered followers, 12 of whom he appointed as his apostles. He was arrested in Jerusalem, tried by the Sanhedrin, and handed over to the Roman authorities, and was crucified on the order of Pontius Pilate.

Christians hold that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day after his death, a belief that became the foundation of the early Christian Church. His first followers were Jews, and the first Christian community was centred in Jerusalem, with Peter, James the brother of Jesus, and John the Apostle among its leaders. After his conversion Paul the Apostle spread his teachings to non-Jewish communities in the eastern Mediterranean. By the end of the 1st century Christianity began to be recognised as a separate religion from Judaism.

Scholars have pursued three quests for the historical Jesus since the 18th century. They agree that he existed, though their portraits differ from each other and from the gospels. Mainstream Judaism rejects the belief that he was the awaited messiah. In Islam he is considered the messiah and a prophet of God, and most Muslims do not believe he was crucified.
jimena-diaz: Jimena, whose name is also spelled Ximena, was born before July 1046. She was the daughter of Diego Fernández, Count of Oviedo, himself the son of Count Fernando Flaínez, and of his wife Cristina, and she was a sister of Fernando Díaz, Count of Asturias. She married Rodrigo Díaz between July 1074 and 12 May 1076.

It is unclear whether she lived with her husband in the Taifa of Zaragoza during his first exile, from 1080 to 1086, when he led the army of its rulers, or whether she went to Asturias in those years. A legal action from Tol dated 1083 suggests that she kept a presence there even while the two were apart. At the start of his second exile, in 1089, she was imprisoned with her children Cristina, Diego and María by order of Alfonso VI. Nothing more is known of her until the end of 1094.

Rodrigo Díaz conquered Valencia on 17 June 1094 and secured it by his victory at the Battle of Cuarte on 21 October, after which Jimena rejoined him and stayed with him until his death. The principality he had founded was an independent state, and she succeeded him as its ruler. Their son Diego had been killed in 1097, fighting under Alfonso VI. A deed of gift that she made to the Cathedral of Valencia in 1101 survives with her signature. When the king judged the city impossible to defend, he escorted her back to Castile.

In 1103 she signed a document at the Monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña selling a monastery she owned to two canons of Burgos. This does not show that she spent her old age in the abbey, as the monastery maintained until the 18th century in the hagiographic texts known as the Legend of Cardeña; it is more likely that she lived her last years in or near Burgos. She died between 29 August 1113 and 1116, probably in 1116.

Through her daughters her descendants entered several ruling houses. Cristina married Ramiro Sánchez of Monzón and was the mother of King García Ramírez of Navarre, and María married first a prince of Aragon and then Ramon Berenguer III, Count of Barcelona. Jimena and her husband were buried at San Pedro de Cardeña. After the tombs were ransacked during the Napoleonic Wars the remains were reburied in Burgos, and they now lie in Burgos Cathedral.
jimmy-carter: James Earl Carter Jr. was born on 1 October 1924 in Plains, Georgia, at the Wise Sanitarium, where his mother worked as a registered nurse. He was the eldest child of Bessie Lillian Gordy and James Earl Carter Sr., a local businessman who ran a general store. The family settled in nearby Archery, a community populated almost entirely by impoverished Black families. His father was staunchly pro-segregation, yet allowed his son to befriend the children of the Black farmhands.

Carter graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1946 and joined the submarine service. In 1952 he began an association with the Navy's nuclear submarine program, led by Captain Hyman G. Rickover, who he later said had the most influence on his life after his parents. He then returned to Plains and expanded the family peanut-growing business.

Carter won a seat in the Georgia State Senate in 1962, after a repeat election because early counting was shown to be the result of fraudulent voting. He served from 1963 to 1967. Sworn in as the 76th governor of Georgia on 12 January 1971, he declared in his inaugural speech that the time for racial discrimination was over, which caused many segregationists who had supported him to feel betrayed. He merged about 300 state agencies into 22.

He announced his presidential campaign on 12 December 1974. Little known outside his home state, he was derided with the question Jimmy Who?. With the Watergate scandal fresh in voters' minds, his position as an outsider helped him, and he narrowly defeated the Republican incumbent Gerald Ford.

Inaugurated on 20 January 1977, Carter issued an unconditional amnesty for Vietnam War draft evaders. His administration negotiated the Camp David Accords, the Panama Canal Treaties and the second Strategic Arms Limitation Talks agreement, established diplomatic relations with China, and created the Departments of Energy and Education. His term was marked by inflation and recession, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran hostage crisis. He lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan in a landslide.

After the presidency Carter established the Carter Center to promote human rights, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002. He travelled widely to conduct peace negotiations, monitor elections and combat neglected tropical diseases, and he was a key figure in Habitat for Humanity. He died at his home in Plains on 29 December 2024, aged 100, and was buried next to his wife Rosalynn. Historians have generally rated his presidency below average, while his post-presidency, the longest in U.S. history, is viewed more favourably.
jin-song-wars: The two powers began as allies. After Wanyan Aguda united the Jurchen tribes and in 1115 named himself emperor of the Jin, the Song emperor Huizong sought his help against the Khitan-led Liao dynasty, hoping to recover the Sixteen Prefectures lost in 938. The Jin took the Liao capitals quickly, while Song attacks on Yanjing failed twice in 1122. By the treaty of 1123 the Song received only seven prefectures and agreed to pay the Jin 300,000 bolts of silk and 200,000 taels of silver a year.

The alliance soon broke down. Zhang Jue, a former Liao governor, turned his city over to the Song, though the treaty forbade harbouring defectors, and in 1124 Song officials asked for nine more prefectures. In November 1125 the Jin emperor Taizong ordered the attack.

Two Jin armies invaded. Kaifeng was first besieged on 31 January 1126, and after 33 days the new emperor Qinzong bought a withdrawal by ceding three prefectures; when he went back on the agreement the Jin returned and broke into the city on 9 January 1127. The Jin then tried to rule the north through puppet states, Da Chu in 1127 and Da Qi from 1130 to 1137. Gaozong, enthroned on 12 June 1127, was pursued as far as the sea in 1130, but the Song navy on the Yangtze and an insurgency in the north checked the invaders.

The peace of 1142 was broken twice. The Jin emperor Wanyan Liang invaded in 1161, was defeated at the Battle of Caishi in November and was assassinated by his own officers in December. Under the Song chancellor Han Tuozhou war was declared on 14 June 1206; the offensive failed, and the treaty of 2 November 1208 raised the tribute. Pressed by the Mongols, the Jin attacked the Song again from 1217 until a peace in 1224 ended the tribute. In 1233 the Song allied with the Mongols, and in 1234 their troops took Caizhou, where the Jin emperor Aizong killed himself.

Some two to three million Jurchens came to rule about 30 million Han Chinese in the north. Over half a million people fled south in 1126–1127. Lin'an, declared the capital in 1138, grew into a major commercial centre. The wars also spurred gunpowder weapons: the fire lance is first reported at the siege of De'an in 1132, and the iron-cased bombs the Jin used at Qizhou in 1221 are the first known hard-casing bombs. After the Jin fell the Mongols turned on the Song, which collapsed in 1279.
joan-of-arc: Joan was born c. 1412 in Domrémy, a small village in the Meuse valley. Her date of birth is unknown. Her parents were Jacques d'Arc and Isabelle Romée, and her father was a peasant farmer with about 20 hectares of land, who also collected taxes and headed the local watch. Joan was not taught to read and write and dictated her letters.

She grew up during the Hundred Years' War, in a France divided between Armagnacs and Burgundians since the Duke of Burgundy had the Duke of Orléans assassinated in 1407. Domrémy's people were loyal to the Armagnac cause. After a raid in 1425 in which cattle were stolen, Joan had her first vision. She later testified that she saw Saint Michael, and later Saint Margaret and Saint Catherine, and that she swore a vow of virginity to these voices.

Joan met Charles VII at Chinon in late February or early March 1429, when she was seventeen and he was twenty-six. Theologians at Poitiers declared her a good Catholic, and women directed by Yolande of Aragon verified her virginity. Charles commissioned plate armor for her, and she designed her own banner.

She reached Orléans on 29 April 1429. At first a figurehead for morale with no formal command, she gained the support of the Armagnac troops and sometimes advised their commanders. On 4 May her arrival rallied soldiers retreating from the bastille of Saint-Loup, and they took it. After the victory at Patay, Charles was crowned at Reims with Joan at his side. The sieges of Paris in September and La Charité in November failed, and her role in these defeats reduced the court's faith in her.

Burgundian troops captured Joan on 23 May 1430, and she was handed to the English in November. Her trial for heresy opened at Rouen on 9 January 1431 under Bishop Pierre Cauchon. She was accused of wearing men's clothes, of acting on demonic visions and of refusing to submit to the church. The trial was politically motivated: her claims, if unchallenged, would undermine the English claim to the French throne. She was burned at the stake on 30 May 1431.

A court reinvestigated the trial in 1456 and overturned the verdict, declaring it tainted by deceit and procedural errors. Joan became a national symbol of France after the French Revolution. She was canonized in 1920 and, two years later, declared one of the patron saints of France.
johann-sebastian-bach: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach on 21 March 1685 (Old Style; 31 March in the new), the eighth and youngest child of Johann Ambrosius Bach, a violinist and director of the town musicians, and Maria Elisabeth, née Lämmerhirt. The Bach family spanned four generations of musicians across Thuringia. Little is known of his early years, and his musical education is largely conjecture: he probably had early instruction from his father and sang with the local schoolboy choir. He studied theology, Latin and Greek at the Latin school, with poor attendance, perhaps because of a string of family deaths: his mother in May 1694 and his father in February 1695.

In 1703 Bach returned to Thuringia and worked as a musician for Protestant churches in Arnstadt and Mühlhausen. He also paid extended visits to the court at Weimar, where he expanded his organ repertory, and to the reformed court at Köthen, where he was mostly engaged with chamber music. By 1723 he was Thomaskantor in Leipzig, responsible for music in four Lutheran city churches and for the St. Thomas School. He decided to compose annual cycles of church cantatas, and wrote for the university's student ensemble, the Collegium Musicum.

Bach began publishing his organ and other keyboard music in 1726. His relations with his employer in Leipzig were difficult, as they had been in some earlier posts. They eased somewhat when Augustus III of Poland granted him the title of court composer of the Elector of Saxony in 1736. In his last decades he reworked and extended many earlier compositions. He died on 28 July 1750, aged 65, of complications following eye surgery. Four of his twenty children, Wilhelm Friedemann, Carl Philipp Emanuel, Johann Christoph Friedrich and Johann Christian, became composers.

Bach's music covers every genre of his time except opera: more than 200 sacred and secular cantatas, oratorios, Passions, motets and Latin church music, a large body of organ and keyboard music, and collections of orchestral and chamber music. He never left modern Germany apart from two brief trips to Bohemia, yet he knew European music widely. He sought to unite Italian and French traditions, particularly the Italian sonata and the French suite, in a mixed style. From about 1712 the music of Antonio Vivaldi was his most important influence.
johann-wolfgang-von-goethe: Goethe's grandfather, Friedrich Georg Goethe, moved to Frankfurt from Thuringia in 1687 and changed the spelling of the family name from Göthe. He worked first as a tailor and then opened a tavern. Goethe's father, Johann Caspar Goethe, had studied law in Leipzig and held the title of Imperial Councillor, but took no part in the official affairs of Frankfurt, then a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. He married Catharina Elisabeth Textor on 20 August 1748. Of their children only Johann Wolfgang and his sister Cornelia survived. The father had the boy taught by private tutors in Latin, Greek, French, Italian and English, as well as dancing, riding and fencing.

His tragedy Götz von Berlichingen (1773) first brought him recognition, and The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774) brought him enormous fame; it is arguably the world's first best-seller. Goethe settled in Weimar in 1775 and was ennobled by Karl August, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, in 1782. He sat on the Duke's privy council from 1776 to 1785, oversaw the reopening of silver mines at Ilmenau and carried out reforms at the University of Jena. After a tour of Italy in 1788 he published his first major scientific work, the Metamorphosis of Plants.

In 1791 he became managing director of the Weimar theatre. From 1794 he was friends with Friedrich Schiller, whose plays he premiered until Schiller's death in 1805. The first part of Faust appeared in 1808. His conversations and shared projects in the 1790s with Schiller, Herder, Fichte and others are collectively termed Weimar Classicism.

Goethe also studied natural science, writing on morphology and colour theory, and he told Johann Peter Eckermann he took more pride in his science of colours than in his poetry. By his death he had gathered 17,800 rock samples. He died in Weimar in 1832 of apparent heart failure. His last words are usually abridged to Mehr Licht!, 'more light', although the earliest account, by Karl Wilhelm Müller, gives a longer request to open a second shutter. Composers including Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt set his poems to music, and the mineral goethite is named after him.
john-f-kennedy: John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born on 29 May 1917 in Brookline, Massachusetts, to Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., a businessman and politician, and Rose Kennedy. His maternal grandfather and namesake, John F. Fitzgerald, was a U.S. congressman and two-term mayor of Boston. He graduated from Harvard University in 1940. Medically disqualified from the Army's Officer Candidate School because of chronic back problems, he joined the United States Naval Reserve on 24 September 1941.

With his father's backing, Kennedy won the Democratic primary for Massachusetts's 11th congressional district in 1946 and sat in the House of Representatives from 1947 to 1953. In 1952 he narrowly defeated Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. for the Senate. After several spinal operations he published Profiles in Courage, which won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography in 1957.

He announced his candidacy for the presidency on 2 January 1960, took the nomination on the first ballot at the Democratic convention in Los Angeles, and chose Lyndon Johnson as his running mate. He was sworn in on 20 January 1961.

Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas at 12:30 p.m. on 22 November 1963, shot as his motorcade passed through Dealey Plaza, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Hospital at 1:00 p.m., aged 46. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested and, on 24 November, shot dead by Jack Ruby before he could be prosecuted. The Warren Commission concluded that Oswald had acted alone, though conspiracy theories persist. Many of Kennedy's proposals passed after his death, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
john-locke: John Locke was born on 29 August 1632 in the village of Wrington, Somerset, to Puritan parents. His father, also John Locke, was an attorney who served as clerk to the Justices of the Peace in Chew Magna, one of whom was Alexander Popham, a Member of Parliament for Bath. Locke was 10 when the English Civil War began, and his father fought for the Parliamentarian side as a captain of cavalry under Popham.

In 1647, under Popham's sponsorship, he became a student at Westminster School in London. Locke wrote of those years, "I found myself in a storm." He then won a place at Christ Church, Oxford, where he spent 15 years, first as a student and then as a tutor, pursuing medical and other scientific interests.

In 1665 Locke travelled outside England for the first time, as secretary to Sir Walter Vane on a failed diplomatic mission to the Elector of Brandenburg. In 1666 he met Anthony Ashley Cooper, later Lord Shaftesbury, and in 1667 moved into Shaftesbury's London home as his personal physician. He studied medicine there under Thomas Sydenham, and was probably instrumental in persuading Shaftesbury to undergo the surgery that saved his life. Locke was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1668.

After Shaftesbury fell from royal favour and died, Locke spent five years in political exile in the Netherlands (1683–85), where he wrote some of his most important works. He returned to England in 1689, served as a Commissioner of Trade and Plantations and retired because of ill health. He is also listed as a shareholder in the Royal Company of Adventures Trading to Africa, which traded in slaves from 1663. He died on 28 October 1704.

In his Letters Concerning Toleration (1689–1692) Locke argued that earthly judges cannot dependably evaluate competing religious truth-claims, that belief cannot be compelled by violence, and that enforcing uniformity would cause more disorder than allowing diversity. In the Essay Concerning Human Understanding he held that the mind is at birth a blank slate, tabula rasa, and that knowledge comes only from experience. He is often credited with describing private property as a natural right, arising when a person mixes labour with nature. The phrase "long train of abuses" in the Declaration of Independence is taken from the Second Treatise.
jorge-luis-borges: Borges was born on 24 August 1899 into an educated middle-class family in Palermo, then a poor area of Buenos Aires. His mother, Leonor Acevedo Suárez, worked as a translator and came from a family of criollo origin that had been much involved in the Argentine War of Independence. In 1914 the family moved to Switzerland, where he studied at the Collège de Genève, and travelled widely in Europe, including Spain. When they returned to Buenos Aires in 1921 he had little formal education and few friends, and he brought with him the doctrine of Ultraism. He began publishing poems and essays in literary journals and worked as a librarian and public lecturer.

Borges's father died in 1938. On Christmas Eve that year Borges suffered a severe head injury and nearly died of sepsis. While recovering he began exploring the new style for which he became known. His first story after the accident, Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote, appeared in May 1939, and his first collection of stories, The Garden of Forking Paths, followed in 1941, composed mostly of works already published in Sur.

Under Juan Perón, he was told he was being promoted from his post at the Miguel Cané Library to inspector of poultry and rabbits at a municipal market; asked why, he was told that he had been on the side of the Allies. He resigned the next day, and the Argentine Society of Writers held a dinner in his honour. In 1955 he was appointed director of the National Public Library and professor of English literature at the University of Buenos Aires. He was completely blind by the age of 55. In 1961 he shared the first International Formentor Prize with Samuel Beckett, and by the 1960s his work was widely translated. He was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

His best-known collections, Ficciones and El Aleph, appeared in the 1940s and explore dreams, labyrinths, chance, infinity, archives, mirrors, fictional writers and mythology. He never wrote a novel; he preferred the short story, finding that a novel required padding. He was also a notable translator from English, French, German, Old English and Old Norse, beginning at ten with a Spanish version of Oscar Wilde's The Happy Prince. He held that a translation may improve upon the original, and that different, even contradictory, renderings can be equally valid. He also practised literary forgery and the review of an imaginary work, a form he drew from Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus.
joseph-stalin: Stalin was born Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili on 18 December 1878 (6 December in the Old Style calendar) in Gori, in the Tiflis Governorate of the Russian Empire. He was the third child of Besarion Jughashvili and Ekaterine Geladze, and the only one to survive infancy. His father's shoemaking workshop declined, the family fell into poverty, and Besarion became an alcoholic who beat his wife and son. In 1894 Stalin enrolled with a scholarship at the Tiflis Theological Seminary as a trainee Orthodox priest, but he lost interest, read Marx and attended secret workers' meetings. He left in April 1899. In November 1901 he was elected to the Tiflis Committee of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party.

After the October Revolution of 1917 Stalin joined Lenin's inner circle and became People's Commissar for Nationalities. After Lenin's death in January 1924 a struggle for the succession followed, in which Stalin used his post as General Secretary to place loyalists across the party and, with Kamenev and Zinoviev, formed a triumvirate against Trotsky.

From 1928 his five-year plans brought rapid collectivisation and industrialisation. State policy contributed to a major famine in the early 1930s, with Ukraine and Kazakhstan most affected. In the Great Purge of 1936–1939 at least 700,000 people were executed and over a million imprisoned in the Gulag. In August 1939 his government signed the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact with Germany, with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe. Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, and the Red Army captured Berlin in 1945.

After the war the Gulag system was expanded further, and by January 1953 three percent of the Soviet population was imprisoned or in internal exile. Stalin died on 5 March 1953 and was succeeded by Nikita Khrushchev, who denounced him and began de-Stalinisation.

Opinion of him remains divided. Most Westerners and anti-communist Russians view him as a mass murderer, significant numbers of Russians and Georgians regard him as a great statesman, and his regime has been widely condemned for mass repression, ethnic cleansing and the deaths of millions.
juan-gines-de-sepulveda: Sepúlveda was born at Pozoblanco in the province of Córdoba, of humble background; his parents were Ginés Sánchez Mellado, a craftsman, and María Ruiz. In 1510 he enrolled at the University of Alcalá de Henares, where he studied philosophy and Greek, and in 1513 he began theology at the College of San Antonio de Sigüenza. In February 1515 he obtained a letter of recommendation from Cardinal Cisneros to the Spanish College in Bologna, where he matriculated that September. There he studied under Pietro Pomponazzi and gained a lifelong expertise in the works of Aristotle, encouraged by his patron Alberto Pío, Prince of Carpi, and by Giulio de' Medici.

By 1523 Sepúlveda had earned doctorates in arts and theology and had taken religious vows as a Dominican priest. When Giulio de' Medici became Pope Clement VII in that year, he served at the papal curia in Rome, where he gained a reputation for scholarship and rhetorical skill. He translated several works of Aristotle from Greek into Latin, among them the Parva Naturalia in 1522 and De mundo in 1523.

He also wrote on the religious controversies of the day: De fato et libero arbitrio against Martin Luther in 1526, De ritu nuptiarum in 1531 against the divorce proceedings of Henry VIII, and the Antapologia against Erasmus in 1532. He despised Luther, but respected Erasmus and corresponded with him for many years. In 1529 he wrote Ad Carolum V, urging Emperor Charles V to unite Europe and fight the Turks.

In Democrates, of 1535, Sepúlveda defended the idea that a just war based on natural law was compatible with Christianity. His case for the conquest drew also on Saint Thomas Aquinas, on the Roman law of just war and the right of conquest, and on the Bible, which he used to justify forced conversion; his position differed from that of the School of Salamanca represented by Francisco de Vitoria. He had never been to America. He claimed that some, though not all, Amerindians were natural slaves as Aristotle defined them in Book I of the Politics, and compared them to children before parents.

Bartolomé de las Casas used the same sources in reply. He held that Christianity should be offered to the natives as an option, not imposed as an obligation, and that no Amerindians lacked the ability to rule themselves. Sepúlveda's later works include histories of the deeds of Charles V, of 1556, and of Philip II, of 1564, and De regno, of 1570. He died on 17 November 1573.
judaism: The term Judaism derives from the Greek Ioudaismos, which first appears in the second century BCE in the book of 2 Maccabees. It meant forming part of a cultural entity, the opposite of Hellenismos, and the conflict between the two lay behind the Maccabean Revolt. According to the Hebrew Bible, God established a covenant with Abraham, who is presented as the ancestor of the Israelites. The Bible tells of a United Kingdom of Israel under Saul, David and Solomon, which split into the Kingdom of Israel and the Kingdom of Judah. Israel fell to the Neo-Assyrian Empire around 720 BCE, and Judah to Nebuchadnezzar II in 586–87 BCE. After the Achaemenid Empire took Babylon, many Israelites returned, and the Second Temple stood until 70 CE.

Judaism is an Abrahamic, monotheistic, ethnic religion. Religious Jews regard it as their means of observing the Mosaic covenant between God and the Jewish people. Its core texts are the Torah, the Nevi'im and the Ketuvim, which together make up the Hebrew Bible, or Tanakh. Alongside this Written Torah stands the Oral Torah, which includes the Mishnah and the Talmud. Rabbinic Judaism holds that God revealed his laws to Moses on Mount Sinai in both forms, and has been the mainstream form since the 6th century CE. The faith begins with ethical monotheism, the belief that God is one, which religious Jews express by reciting the Shema Yisrael twice daily.

Christianity was originally a sect of Second Temple Judaism, and the two religions diverged in the first century, at first over whether Jesus was the Jewish Messiah. Judaism's texts, traditions and values strongly influenced Christianity and Islam, and through Christianity it has had an indirect but significant role in Western culture. The Jewish Enlightenment of the late 18th century divided Western Jewry into the Orthodox, Conservative and Reform movements. Daniel Boyarin argues that Judaism does not fit conventional Western categories such as religion, ethnicity or culture.
julius-caesar: Gaius Julius Caesar was born into a patrician family, the gens Julia, on 12 or 13 July 100 BCE. The family claimed descent from Julus, the son of Aeneas, and so from Venus. There is no evidence that Caesar was born by Caesarian section, since such operations entailed the mother's death and his mother lived for decades afterwards. The Julii Caesares were not especially influential in the middle republic; their first consul held office in 157 BCE. Caesar's father, of the same name, married Aurelia, and his sister married the influential Gaius Marius.

Caesar won the consulship of 59 BCE with the support of Crassus. He reconciled Pompey and Crassus in a three-way alliance, termed the First Triumvirate in modern times. His victories in the Gallic Wars, completed by 51 BCE, greatly expanded Roman territory; during them he invaded Britain and built a bridge across the Rhine. From 52 to 49 BCE trust between Caesar and Pompey disintegrated. On 7 January 49 BCE the Senate declared Caesar an enemy, and in early January he crossed the Rubicon and marched towards Rome, beginning the civil war.

He was appointed dictator some four times from 49 BCE and annually from April 46 BCE. The Senate gave him honours, among them his portrait on coins, as the first living Roman so shown, and the renaming of Quintilis as Julius. He created the Julian calendar, settled veterans in overseas colonies and extended citizenship to communities in Spain and northern Italy. He took the title dictator perpetuo in February 44 BCE.

A group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius, fearful of his power and of the possibility that he might make himself king, assassinated Caesar on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE. New civil wars followed and the Republic's constitutional government was never fully restored. His great-nephew and adoptive heir Octavian, later Augustus, rose to sole power thirteen years later and became the first emperor. Much of Caesar's life is known from his own commentaries, the Gallic Wars and the Civil War, which he wrote with his political career in mind. His name became a title, giving rise to Kaiser and Tsar.
